title: Validating Input and Reporting Errors
summary: Check every request at the edge, decide between 400, 409, and 422, and answer every error in one Problem Details format.
intro: Everything a client sends is just text, and some of it is wrong: a typo, a phone app two versions behind, a script written in a hurry, and now and then a person poking for weaknesses. An API that trusts what arrives ends up storing a booking for minus five people, crashing on a date it can't read, or answering with an error so vague nobody can fix their request. This lesson shows you how to check every request where it enters, with a schema for each body and query string, where each kind of check belongs, and which status code each failure earns. Then it gives every error one shape, the Problem Details format, built in one central place in Spring.

steps.title: Never trust input
steps.body:
Your server can't see who is on the other end. A request from Roombook's own web app looks just like one typed into curl, and anyone can type into curl. So every part of a request, its path, query string, headers, and body, is input from outside, and could be anything at all. It goes wrong in two ways:

- **Wrong by mistake**: a misspelled field, a date in the wrong format, a number sent as text, an end time before the start, or a client built against last year's version of the API.
- **Hostile on purpose**: a fifty-megabyte body, a note of a million characters, an id of `-1` or `99999999999999999999`, or a field nobody should be able to set, like `"isAdmin": true`, or `"status": "confirmed"` on a booking that broke the rules.

## Parse at the edge

The answer is to check everything in one place: the **edge** of your API, where requests come in, before any of your own code uses them. Picture a line drawn around your server's code, called the **trust boundary**. Outside the line is text from strangers. Inside are values your code can rely on.

```diagram validation-and-errors-trust
Text from outside is checked once, at the boundary, and only typed values go further in.
```

Crossing the line is the job of **parsing**: turning text into typed values, or refusing. A parser for a booking doesn't just answer yes or no. It hands back a booking whose `attendees` is a whole number from 1 to 30, whose times are real moments in UTC, and which has no fields nobody expected. Code inside the line takes that value and never checks those things again. The idea has a slogan: **parse, don't validate**. Checking the text and then passing the text on leaves every later function wondering whether it was checked. Passing on the parsed value makes the checking part of the type.

A **schema** is how you describe a valid input: each field, its type, whether it's required, and its limits. A schema library reads a request against it and gives back either the typed value or a list of everything that's wrong.

## Why Java's types aren't enough

Java's types do check something at run time. Jackson, the JSON library Spring uses, refuses to put `"lots"` into an `Integer`, and the request fails. But a type only says what kind of value fits, not which values make sense. `-5` is a perfectly good `Integer`, and an end time an hour before the start is a perfectly good `Instant`. And by Spring Boot's default settings, a field the record doesn't have, like `isAdmin`, is quietly dropped, so a client never learns its field was ignored. The example shows a record with no checks taking all of that.

So Spring adds **Bean Validation**, a Java standard for checks written as annotations, like `@Min(1)` on a field. Hibernate Validator is the library that runs them, and Spring Boot's validation starter brings it in.

examples.title: A handler that trusts its input
examples.prompt: This controller takes a `BookingInput` record with no checks on it, and answers `201` with the record. Send it a booking that breaks every rule.
examples.explanation: Jackson read every value into the record's types without complaint, and the controller answered 201. The booking ends an hour before it starts, has minus five people, and `isAdmin` vanished without a word, since the record has no such field. Send `"attendees": "lots"` instead, and Jackson does refuse it, with a 400 whose detail just says `Failed to read request`. So the types caught the one mistake that breaks the format, and none of the ones that break the rules. The fix is Bean Validation on the record, and `@Valid` on the parameter, so Spring checks the values too.

steps.title: Schemas for request bodies

examples.title: Normalized on the way in
examples.prompt: Book Turing with a start time two hours ahead of UTC, and a note with spaces around it.
examples.code: curl -s localhost:8080/v1/bookings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"roomId": 1, "startsAt": "2026-10-05T16:00:00+02:00", "endsAt": "2026-10-05T15:30:00Z", "attendees": 3, "note": "  Algorithms study group  "}'
examples.explanation: The request said `16:00:00+02:00`, and the stored booking says `14:00:00Z`: the same moment, now in UTC, so every later comparison, like checking for overlaps, compares like with like. The spaces around the note are gone. The rest of the booking comes from the service and the store, which the next lesson builds: an id, the user, a status, a version, and when it was created, which is the course's fixed clock. None of those were the client's to set, and the schema made sure they weren't.

examples.title: Several mistakes, one answer
examples.prompt: Send a booking with several things wrong at once.
examples.output: {"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","status":422,"title":"Validation failed","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","errors":[{"field":"attendees","message":"must be greater than or equal to 1"},{"field":"roomId","message":"must be greater than 0"},{"field":"startsAt","message":"must not be null"}],"requestId":"e817f00f-bc73-4bce-9286-35a47ae27176"}
examples.explanation: This body converts cleanly, so Bean Validation ran and reported all three broken rules at once: the start time is missing, the room id is 0, and there are no attendees. The messages are Hibernate Validator's defaults. Send the body with `"roomId": "1"`, `"startsAt": "next monday"`, and an extra `notes`, and you get just one error, `roomId` with `has the wrong type`, because Jackson stops at the first value it can't convert and Bean Validation never runs. Clients fix those one at a time. The shape of the whole answer is part 5's subject.

steps.title: Path, query, and header values

examples.title: A query string over its limits
examples.prompt: Ask for rooms with a minimum capacity of 0 and a limit over the maximum.
examples.output: {"detail":"2 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/rooms","status":422,"title":"Validation failed","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","errors":[{"field":"minCapacity","message":"must be greater than or equal to 1"},{"field":"limit","message":"must be less than or equal to 100"}],"requestId":"3c3fc09f-3d3c-4e8d-ad69-97cb912061cd"}
examples.explanation: Both broken limits come back at once, in the same shape as the body errors in part 2, so a client handles both with the same code. Ask for `minCapacity=lots` instead, and you get only `minCapacity` with `has the wrong type`, even with `limit=500` beside it, because a value that won't convert stops the record from being built, so the other checks never run.

examples.title: An id that names nothing
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking whose id isn't a number.
examples.explanation: A path that can't name a booking is a 404, the same answer as a booking id that's a number but doesn't exist. To the client, both mean there's nothing at that URL, so there's no reason to tell them apart, and no reason to say how ids are checked. The `type` is Roombook's `not-found` problem, the same for every 404.

steps.title: Where each check belongs

examples.title: Three broken rules
examples.prompt: Book Lovelace, which holds four, for five people, starting at a quarter past and lasting three and three quarter hours.
examples.output: {"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","status":422,"title":"Validation failed","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","errors":[{"field":"startsAt","message":"must be on the hour or half past"},{"field":"endsAt","message":"a booking lasts 30 minutes to 3 hours"},{"field":"attendees","message":"Lovelace holds at most 4 people"}],"requestId":"e7537fb3-16b3-4bf0-a81d-52c727bb3279"}
examples.explanation: The body passed the schema: every field had the right type and range. Then the service found three broken rules and reported all of them, in the same shape as the schema's errors: the start isn't on the hour or half past, the booking is longer than three hours, and Lovelace holds four. It's a 422, since this request is wrong no matter what anyone else has booked. Only the request can be fixed, and the messages say exactly what to change.

examples.title: A booking that clashes
examples.prompt: With Ada's 14:00 to 15:30 booking of Turing already made, book Turing from 15:00 to 16:00.
examples.explanation: Every field and every rule was fine, so the request reached the store, which found the overlap with the existing booking and refused. It's a 409, with its own type, `booking-overlap`, so a client can tell it apart from every other conflict and offer to show the room's free times. The same request succeeds once the other booking is cancelled, which is what makes it a conflict and not a 422. From the data integrity lesson on, the database finds the overlap, and the answer stays exactly the same.

steps.title: One error format: Problem Details

examples.title: A problem, headers and all
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking that doesn't exist, and look at the headers as well as the body.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 
X-Request-Id: bfecbc97-1f02-4158-931c-48ad335dfab0
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:50 GMT

{"detail":"No booking with id 1999.","instance":"/v1/bookings/1999","status":404,"title":"Resource not found","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/not-found","requestId":"bfecbc97-1f02-4158-931c-48ad335dfab0"}
examples.explanation: The headers say what the body is before a client reads a byte of it: `application/problem+json`. The body has the standard members in Jackson's order, with `not-found` as the type, the same one every 404 in Roombook uses, and the detail saying which booking. `requestId` matches the `X-Request-Id` header, so whoever reports the error can quote it.

steps.title: Central error handling

examples.title: Broken JSON
examples.prompt: Send a body that stops halfway through.
examples.output: {"detail":"The body couldn't be parsed as JSON.","instance":"/v1/bookings","status":400,"title":"Body is not valid JSON","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/invalid-json","requestId":"56ef973a-a4a0-4b7a-a9d7-efd663c19cb5"}
examples.explanation: Jackson couldn't parse the body, Spring threw `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, and since the cause wasn't a field problem, Roombook's override answered the `invalid-json` problem. It's a 400, not a 422, because there's no content to judge: the server couldn't read the request at all. Spring's own detail, `Failed to read request`, is replaced with one that says what to fix.

examples.title: A crash, answered safely
examples.prompt: Ask for a test route whose handler fails with `connection to the database was lost`.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 500 
X-Request-Id: 9037482b-b403-4494-a713-89a2504afcd1
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:50 GMT
Connection: close

{"detail":"Something went wrong on our side. Quote the request id if you report it.","instance":"/v1/crash","status":500,"title":"Internal server error","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/internal-error","requestId":"9037482b-b403-4494-a713-89a2504afcd1"}
examples.explanation: The client gets the generic `internal-error` problem and the request id, and not a word about the database. The server's terminal has the rest: an `ERROR` line with the same id in brackets, and the stack trace. Anyone who reports the error can quote the id, and whoever fixes it can find those lines in seconds. Tomcat closes the connection after a 500, as `Connection: close` says, in case the error left it in a bad state.

examples.title: A method the route doesn't have
examples.prompt: Try to delete the list of rooms, a path that only answers GET.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405 
X-Request-Id: fcd0a1de-7546-4842-85e3-47158388ee13
Allow: GET
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:50 GMT

{"detail":"Method 'DELETE' is not supported.","instance":"/v1/rooms","status":405,"title":"Method not allowed","type":"https://roombook.example/problems/method-not-allowed","requestId":"fcd0a1de-7546-4842-85e3-47158388ee13"}
examples.explanation: Spring threw `HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException`, and the base class answered with 405 and an `Allow` header listing what the path does take. Its body went through `createResponseEntity`, so `complete()` filled in Roombook's `method-not-allowed` type and title, and added `instance` and `requestId`. Every one of Spring's own errors gets the same treatment with no extra code. The next lesson moves the booking rules into a service of their own, and wires the layers together.

recap:
- Every part of a request is untrusted text, so parse it at the edge into typed values, and pass only those inward.
- Java's types check kinds of values, not their meaning, so Bean Validation checks what actually arrives.
- A schema checks types, formats, ranges, and lengths, refuses unknown fields, and normalizes values, like times to UTC.
- Each operation gets its own schema, since create, replace, and patch need different fields.
- Query and path values are text too: convert them, give them defaults, and bound anything that costs the server work.
- Shape is checked at the edge, business rules in the service, and races in the database.
- 400 means unreadable, 422 means readable but invalid, and 409 means valid but in conflict with current data.
- Every error is a Problem Details object with a stable type, built in one central handler, and a 500 never reveals internals.
